title: Popcorn Ceiling Removal and Asbestos: Test First
description: Popcorn ceilings installed before the mid-1980s may contain asbestos. How testing works, what to do with the results, and how safe removal is done.
h1: Popcorn Ceiling Removal and Asbestos: What You Must Know First
heroIntro: Textured ceilings from before the mid-1980s can contain asbestos, and scraping them dry releases fibers into your home. The first tool for this job is a lab test, not a scraper.
excerpt: Older popcorn ceilings may contain asbestos. How testing works, what the results mean, and how safe removal is actually done.

secondary: does my popcorn ceiling have asbestos
questions: How do I know if my popcorn ceiling has asbestos?
Is it safe to scrape a popcorn ceiling myself?

sections.h2: Why older popcorn ceilings are a concern
body: Spray-on acoustic texture, often called popcorn or cottage cheese ceiling, was popular for decades because it hid drywall flaws and was quick to apply. Some of the products used before the mid-1980s contained asbestos fibers. The material was largely phased out of these products after the late 1970s, but existing stock continued to be installed for some time, so a home built or remodeled into the 1980s may still have it.

Asbestos in a ceiling that is intact and left alone is generally considered a low risk. The danger comes when the material is disturbed: dry scraping, sanding, or drilling releases microscopic fibers that can stay in the air, settle into carpet and ductwork, and be inhaled. Asbestos exposure is linked to serious lung diseases that can appear decades later. You cannot tell whether texture contains asbestos by looking at it.

sections.h2: Step one: get the texture tested
body: Testing is straightforward and is the only reliable way to know. Results usually come back within days, and the lab report states whether asbestos was detected and at what percentage. Any contractor you hire has to follow state and federal asbestos rules, and disposal of asbestos-containing waste is regulated, so a written result protects everyone involved and tells the contractor how the job must be handled. Many reputable painting and drywall contractors will not scrape an untested ceiling in an older home, and that is a good sign rather than an inconvenience. You have two options for getting samples to a lab:
bullets: Hire a licensed asbestos inspector or consultant to take samples and send them to an accredited laboratory. This is the best choice if you are selling, remodeling extensively, or want documentation.
Take a sample yourself using a mail-in kit processed by an accredited lab, following the instructions closely.

sections.h2: If you take your own sample
body: Sampling disturbs only a small area, but treat it carefully:
bullets: Turn off the HVAC system and close the room off; keep children and pets out.
Wear a disposable N95 or better respirator, gloves, and eye protection.
Lightly mist the spot with water mixed with a drop of dish soap to keep dust down.
Cut out a small piece, through the full depth of the texture, into a sealable bag.
Sample more than one room if the texture may have been applied at different times, since ceilings in additions and remodeled areas can differ.
Patch the spot with spackle or tape, and wipe the area with a damp cloth. Do not vacuum with a household vacuum.

sections.h2: If the test is negative: how removal is done
body: A clean result means the ceiling can be removed using standard methods. The work is messy but not complicated:
bullets: Remove furniture or cover it completely. Cover floors and walls in plastic, and tape off vents, outlets, and fixtures. Turn off the power to ceiling fixtures.
Lightly mist a section of ceiling with water and let it soak for several minutes so the texture softens.
Scrape with a wide, rounded-corner scraper, working in manageable sections. Avoid gouging the drywall face.
If the texture was painted over, water will not penetrate as easily; scoring or a stripping solution may be needed.
Once the texture is off, repair the drywall: re-tape loose seams, then skim coat the ceiling to create a smooth surface. Most ceilings that had popcorn were never finished smooth underneath.
Sand, prime with a drywall primer, and finish with two coats of flat ceiling paint.

sections.h2: If the test is positive: your options
body: Do not scrape it. If asbestos is present, you generally have three choices:
bullets: Leave it alone if it is intact and you do not plan work that disturbs it.

Encapsulate it: seal it with a suitable coating, or cover it with new drywall fastened through to the joists, which leaves the material in place but protected. This avoids removal but should be planned carefully, since drilling and fastening still disturbs small areas.
Have it removed by a licensed asbestos abatement contractor, who will contain the area, use negative air pressure, and dispose of the material according to regulations.

body: Removal is not the only way to get rid of a dated ceiling. If the texture tested clear but you would rather avoid the mess, a new layer of thin ceiling drywall can be installed over it and finished smooth, which also works for ceilings that are cracked or stained. Some homeowners simply repaint the existing texture to brighten it. Use a thick-nap roller and a flat ceiling paint, roll in one direction with light pressure, and test a small area first, since the moisture in paint can soften old texture and pull it loose in sheets.
In a humid Florida home, keep in mind that popcorn texture traps dust and can show mildew spotting in bathrooms and rooms with poor airflow. Improving ventilation helps whichever route you choose.

sections.h2: Lead paint and other hidden issues
body: In homes built before 1978, the paint on top of the popcorn texture may contain lead. If the ceiling has been painted, include a lead test in your plans. Ceilings can also hide water stains, sagging drywall, or loose tape, which show up once the texture is gone. A ceiling with a history of leaks should have the source fixed before any finishing work; our article on urgent drywall repair covers water-damaged board.

Removing a tested, asbestos-free ceiling is possible as a DIY project, but it is physically demanding, dusty, and the skim coat is a skill that takes practice to get right. A smooth, flat ceiling is unforgiving under modern lighting.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my popcorn ceiling has asbestos?
faqs.a: Only a laboratory test can tell. Ceilings applied before the mid-1980s are the main concern, but age alone is not proof either way. Use an accredited lab, either through a licensed inspector or a mail-in sample kit.

faqs.q: Is it safe to remove popcorn ceiling myself?
faqs.a: If the texture has tested negative for asbestos, and lead if it was painted, DIY removal is possible with good dust control and protective equipment. If it tests positive, do not scrape it; leave it intact, encapsulate it, or hire a licensed abatement contractor.

faqs.q: Can I paint over a popcorn ceiling that contains asbestos?
faqs.a: Painting can help encapsulate intact texture, but rolling can loosen popcorn and release material. Get advice from an asbestos professional before painting a positive-testing ceiling.

faqs.q: What happens to the ceiling after the popcorn is removed?
faqs.a: The drywall underneath usually needs seam repair and a skim coat to make it smooth, followed by sanding, primer, and two coats of flat ceiling paint.
